name: Diego Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing physiotherapy, so a normal week is anatomy lectures, practical sessions where we learn to massage and mobilise joints on each other, and a lot of memorising muscles. I live at home with my mum and my grandmother, and on Saturdays and Sundays I pick orders at a distribution centre out by the motorway, ten hours a day on my feet. I got top grades, mostly because I'm stubborn about studying. I like things I can do with my hands, and I don't really use apps or chatbots if I can avoid them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, no big deal. People have been saying computers will take over for years and my warehouse still has humans in it. I'd say physio is hands-on, so nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd just carry on. My worry isn't AI, it's whether I can afford the next three years. My loan covers fees but not the bus, my books or my phone, and the warehouse shifts are all I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the warehouse job, study hard and aim for a clinical placement in the second year. I wouldn't change anything about how I work. I'd keep everything on paper if I can, because I remember better that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, but tight. It's like walking along a wall: it's okay as long as I don't look down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the warehouse is ten hours on your feet. How does that fit with study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse has started using handheld scanners that tell us the route. My supervisor, Kofi, says it's smarter. All I know is that on Sundays my legs are done by four and my notes from Saturday are still unread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the cost of everything. My mum earns just above the line where she gets help, and my grandmother needs her tablets. If prices went up and the warehouse cut hours, we'd all feel it at once.

say: I'd say it's **fine**: people have said computers will take over for years, and my warehouse still has humans.
I'd say physio is **hands-on**, so nothing changes.
think: Privately, I just carry on; my worry is whether I can **afford** the next three years.
The loan covers fees, but not the **bus**, books or phone.
do: Keep the **warehouse** job, study hard and aim for a clinical placement in second year.
Keep notes on **paper**, because I remember better that way.
feel: **Fine** but tight, like walking along a wall.
S0.quote: On Sundays my legs are done by four and my notes from Saturday are still unread.
fieldNote: His **money** pressure is real: a warehouse weekend, a mother just above the help line and a grandmother's tablets.
Does not use AI at all; treats the plateau as normal life.

steps.text: Keep the weekend shifts at the distribution centre
Aim for a clinical placement in second year
Cut my phone plan and bus top-ups to save money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software will do the booking and the notes, and maybe the exercise sheets. The part where you put your hands on someone and feel what's wrong, that's ours. I'd say learn the hands first and the screens later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be uneasy. The jobs near me are the physio clinics, and if a clinic makes do with fewer receptionists and assistants, there'd be fewer places for students to start. I'm not good with new systems, and the first time a program does my job better I'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder on the hands-on side and get extra practice from older physios. I'd start using the clinic software only when the placement forces me to. And I'd keep the warehouse shifts, because the pay is predictable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Edgy. I don't like feeling that I'm behind before I've even started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of physiotherapy do you think software might take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum it's slow and the job isn't going anywhere, which is what I believe on a good day. Then I'd quietly check how much I owe. She worries about things I don't say, so I try to say less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse, because the scanners are already telling us what to do. If it spreads to robots picking the boxes, my weekend job could go. I'd need a plan, but I'd probably wait until it's obvious.

say: I'd say software handles **booking** and notes, but the hands-on part is ours.
I'd say learn the **hands** first and the screens later.
think: Privately, I'm **uneasy**: fewer clinic assistants could mean fewer places for students to start.
I'm bad with new systems and would feel it when a program does it **better**.
do: Get extra **practice** on the hands-on side from older physios.
Use clinic software only when a **placement** forces me to, and keep the warehouse shifts.
feel: **Edgy**, as if I'm behind before I've started.
S1.quote: The part where you put your hands on someone and feel what's wrong, that's ours.
fieldNote: He trusts **hands-on** work but admits that clinic admin and entry-level places could shrink.
Plans to wait until he is forced, which fits a resistant temperament and leaves him exposed.

steps.text: Ask older physios for extra hands-on practice sessions
Keep the warehouse weekend shifts for steady pay
Wait until a placement requires the clinic software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of noise and I'd believe it when I see it. Then I'd go quiet and look at what it means for the warehouse. I'd tell friends to keep studying because nobody knows what happens next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be rattled. Two years from now I'm halfway through the degree, and the robots for hands-on work arrive in about five. My mum and gran depend on the warehouse's kind of work being around, and so do I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every shift I can, put every spare pound into my savings account and talk to my tutor about what the degree is worth. I'd ask the union rep at the warehouse what happens if robots replace pickers. I'd go to the careers office, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened and a bit stuck. I don't have a plan and I don't have any money to make one with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the day after you heard it was two years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My gran would say God provides, and my mum would say we've been through worse, and neither would sleep. I'd pretend it's fine in front of them and then lie awake. It's not a good habit, but it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your mum and grandmother take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I've got a hands-on degree, which should give me about three extra years, but my family doesn't have three extra years of money. The robots could take the warehouse job long before they get near a physio's table.

say: I'd say it's **noise** and I'll believe it when I see it, and tell friends to keep studying.
I'd ask the **union** rep what happens if robots replace pickers.
think: Privately, I'd be **rattled**: I'd be halfway through the degree and the warehouse job could go first.
I have no **plan** and no money to make one.
do: Work every **shift** I can and put every spare pound into savings.
Visit the **careers** office and ask my tutor what the degree is worth.
feel: **Frightened** and stuck; no plan and no money to make one.
S2.quote: The robots could take the warehouse job long before they get near a physio's table.
fieldNote: He says it is noise, yet the **warehouse** job that pays his bus fare is the first thing at risk.
Shows the gap between a calm public line and a private panic, with no savings to cushion it.

steps.text: Work every available shift at the distribution centre
Ask the warehouse union rep about robot pickers
Visit the university careers office for the first time
Stay in the degree and ask the tutor about its worth

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still dramatic, but at least it's far enough that I'd finish my degree before I find out. I'd tell friends to keep going and not panic. It's the sort of thing that's easier to ignore, and that's my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel like I have a chance. Five years to graduate, and the hands-on robots come three years after that. That gives me a gap where physio is still a person's job, and I can work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study, take every placement and learn to do assessments quickly and well. I'd start a small saving habit, maybe thirty pounds a month. And I'd finally try one of those AI tools if my tutor shows it works for notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Not good, but better. It feels like a hill I can climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is more time. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum and gran, who would be in a world where care is more important and the NHS is under pressure. If robots help with lifting, maybe they'd get better care. I'd like to be the one doing it, not the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be harder to deal with than in the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my pride. I don't like admitting I'd need to learn a tool. But if I see it working for my tutor, I'd cope. I don't hate technology, I just don't trust it until I've watched it do something right.

say: I'd tell friends to keep going and **not panic**, because it is far enough away.
I'd say we should finish the **degree** first.
think: Privately, I'd feel I have a **chance**: five years to graduate, and hands-on robots come three years after.
That gap lets me **work** as a physio.
do: Take every **placement** and save thirty pounds a month.
Try an AI tool for **notes** only if my tutor shows it works.
feel: **Better**, not good; a hill I can climb.
S3.quote: I don't hate technology, I just don't trust it until I've watched it do something right.
fieldNote: The longer timeline gives him a **window** where physio is still a person's job.
Remains anxious about money; his resistance softens only when a trusted tutor demonstrates a tool.

steps.text: Take every clinical placement offered by the degree
Save thirty pounds a month from warehouse pay
Try an AI notes tool once my tutor shows it works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and I'd be getting on with my career. I'd tell friends not to lose sleep, and to keep learning a trade they can use. It's the one scenario where I wouldn't change a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's the best of the five. I'd qualify, work as a physio for six or seven years and maybe pay off the loan. I could even set up my own clinic in my gran's neighbourhood before robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work in the NHS for a few years and then look at private practice. I'd stay away from tech if I can, but I'd learn whatever the clinic requires. I'd also put my mum on a better savings plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. I'd still be tired from the work, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you want to have done by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry the world has less patience for people who need hands-on help. Robots could do a lot of the lifting, and older patients might prefer a person. I'd want to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you even with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's pension. She's cleaned hospital wards for twenty years and she's got little saved. Ten years is plenty of time to build it up, if prices stay sane. That's the part I can't control.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** and tell friends not to lose sleep.
I'd say keep learning a **trade** you can use.
think: Privately, it's the **best** of the five: I'd qualify, work for years and maybe pay off the loan.
I could even set up my own **clinic** before robots arrive.
do: Finish the degree, work in the NHS and then look at **private** practice.
Learn whatever the clinic requires and put my mum on a better **savings** plan.
feel: Pretty **calm**; tired from work but not scared.
S4.quote: I could even set up my own clinic in my gran's neighbourhood before robots come.
fieldNote: With ten years the **degree** pays off in his mind and he can picture his own clinic.
His one concern is his mother's thin **pension**, not his own job.

steps.text: Finish the degree and work in the NHS
Open my own physio clinic near my gran's home
Move mum's savings into a better account

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened? And is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd be halfway through a degree with no money behind me, and a warehouse job that robots could take first. What would help is a way to keep studying without needing the weekend shifts, and some real notice before anything changes. One thing you didn't ask: I never say any of this at home. My gran thinks I'm going to be a doctor and I'm not going to be the one to tell her the plan is shaky.

headlineQuote: My gran thinks I'm going to be a doctor and I'm not going to be the one to tell her the plan is shaky.
portrait: Diego is a **physiotherapy** student who lives with his mum and grandmother and picks orders at a warehouse every weekend.
He is stubborn about studying, avoids AI entirely and trusts only what he has **watched** work.
Centre in outlook, he says little at home and carries the **money** worries alone.
Calm with ten years to prepare, but with two years the weekend job and a thin cushion leave him **alarmed**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case worries him most: halfway through the degree, with no money and a warehouse job at risk.
whatWouldHelp: A way to keep studying without **weekend** shifts and real notice before anything changes.
